lesson.title: Cutting the Data Into Quarters: Meet Q1 and Q3
lesson.summary: Quartiles split an ordered data set into four equal-sized groups, giving you three landmark values, Q1, the median, and Q3, that describe the middle of a distribution in more detail than the median alone.
lesson.body:
The median tells you where the center of a data set sits, but it says nothing about how spread out the values around that center are. Quartiles fix that gap. They are simply specific percentiles: the first quartile, Q1, is the 25th percentile, the median is the 50th percentile, and the third quartile, Q3, is the 75th percentile. Together they divide an ordered list of data into four groups of roughly equal size, so about a quarter of the data falls below Q1, about half falls below the median, and about three quarters falls below Q3.

The most common way to find quartiles by hand, and the method used throughout an AP Statistics course, works in three steps. First, arrange the data from smallest to largest and locate the median, which splits the data into a lower half and an upper half. Second, if the number of values, n, is odd, exclude the median itself from both halves before continuing; if n is even, the two halves already split cleanly. Third, find the median of the lower half to get Q1, and the median of the upper half to get Q3.

Consider twelve quiz scores, already sorted: 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80, 83, 85, 88, 92. Since n equals 12, an even number, the median is the average of the 6th and 7th values, 75 and 78, which gives (75 + 78) divided by 2, or 76.5. The lower half consists of the first six scores: 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75. The median of that half is the average of its 3rd and 4th values, 68 and 70, which gives 69. That is Q1. The upper half consists of the last six scores: 78, 80, 83, 85, 88, 92. Its median is the average of 83 and 85, which gives 84. That is Q3.

The distance between Q3 and Q1 is called the interquartile range, or IQR. In this example, IQR equals 84 minus 69, or 15 points. That single number tells you the width of the middle 50 percent of quiz scores, a much more stable description of spread than the full range, since the IQR is not dragged around by one unusually high or low score the way the range or the mean can be.

It helps to double check the percentile framing directly against this example. Twelve scores means each value represents about 8.3 percent of the data, so Q1 at 69 has roughly three scores at or below it, close to the target of one quarter, and Q3 at 84 has roughly nine scores at or below it, close to the target of three quarters. With small data sets like this one, the match to exact percentiles is only approximate, since twelve values cannot be split into perfectly even quarters, but the method still gives a consistent, repeatable answer, which is exactly what a shared definition of quartiles is meant to provide.

Quartiles matter because they set up nearly every tool used later to summarize and compare distributions. The five-number summary is built directly from the minimum, Q1, the median, Q3, and the maximum. Boxplots are just a picture of those five numbers. And the 1.5 times IQR rule, which flags unusually extreme values as outliers, depends entirely on knowing Q1 and Q3 first. Getting comfortable finding quartiles by hand, and understanding what they represent as percentiles, is the foundation for all of that work.
